title: Manaslu Restricted Area Permit: Fees, Rules, How to Apply
meta_description: Manaslu restricted area permit 2026: fees by season, Tsum Valley permit, MCAP and ACAP, licensed guide rule, solo trekker change and how agencies apply.
summary: To trek the Manaslu Circuit you need the Manaslu restricted area permit, issued only through a registered agency, plus the Manaslu and Annapurna conservation area permits and a local fee. A licensed guide is mandatory. In 2026 Nepal dropped the two-trekker minimum, so solo trekkers can now apply. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Why Manaslu is a restricted area
paras: Northern Gorkha borders Tibet, and Nepal controls access to its border districts through restricted area permits issued by the Department of Immigration. The upper Budhi Gandaki, from around Jagat to the Larkya La and down to the Manang district side, falls inside the Manaslu restricted area. The Tsum Valley, east of the main trail, has its own permit. The rules aim to manage numbers, protect fragile communities and make sure trekkers in remote border country are accompanied.

In practice this means you cannot simply turn up and walk. The permit must be applied for in Kathmandu by a government-registered trekking agency, for a fixed itinerary and dates, before you set off. Your guide carries the permit and presents it at checkpoints in Jagat, Philim, Namrung and Samagaun areas, and your conservation permits are also checked.

sections.heading: Permit fees at a glance
paras: Fees below are those we understand to apply in 2026. They are charged per person, and the restricted area permits are calculated for the days you spend inside the restricted zone, not the whole trek. Rates have changed several times in recent years, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The guide rule and the 2026 solo change
paras: For years the Manaslu permit came with two conditions: at least two foreign trekkers had to apply together, and they had to be accompanied by a licensed guide from a registered agency. Solo trekkers often had to pay for a phantom second permit or join a stranger's group to qualify.

On 22 March 2026, according to a notice from Nepal's Department of Immigration reported by several trekking operators, the two-person minimum was removed across all restricted trekking areas, including Manaslu and Tsum. Solo trekkers can now apply individually. The guide requirement has not changed: every trekker, alone or in a group, must still walk with a government-licensed guide arranged through a registered agency. Fully independent trekking remains prohibited. As with all permit rules, check current status before you travel.
list: Two-person minimum: removed in 2026, as we understand it
Licensed guide: still mandatory for every trekker
Registered agency: still required to apply for the permit
Independent trekking: not allowed in the restricted area

sections.heading: How the application works
paras: You do not apply yourself. Your agency submits the application to the Department of Immigration in Kathmandu with your documents, the itinerary, the guide's details and insurance information. Because the permit is linked to your Nepal visa, it is normally issued after you arrive and obtain your visa, usually on the working day before you drive to Machha Khola. Immigration offices close on Saturdays and public holidays, which can affect timing.

Send your agency clear scans of the documents a few weeks in advance so they can prepare the conservation permits and check your details. On arrival you hand over your passport for a few hours, or the agency uses your original once your visa is stamped. The permit is printed with your name, passport number, dates and route, and your guide keeps the original during the trek.
list: Passport valid for at least six months, with a Nepal visa covering your trek dates
Passport-size photos, or digital photos for the online system
Travel insurance covering helicopter evacuation to at least 6,000 m
Fixed itinerary with entry and exit dates
Details of your licensed guide and registered agency

sections.heading: Which permits for which trek
paras: The standard Manaslu Circuit from Machha Khola to Dharapani needs the Manaslu restricted area permit, both conservation area permits and the municipality fee. A trek that goes only to Samagaun and returns the same way, or flies out by helicopter, needs the Manaslu permits but not the Annapurna one. A Tsum Valley trek alone needs the Tsum restricted area permit, the Manaslu Conservation Area Permit and the local fee. Combining Tsum and Manaslu needs both restricted area permits.

Helicopter tours that land in Samagaun also need the Manaslu restricted area permit for each foreign passenger, even for a 45-minute stop. Peak climbs such as Larkya Peak add a Nepal Mountaineering Association climbing permit and a refundable garbage deposit on top of the trekking permits.

sections.heading: Indian and SAARC nationals
paras: Indian passport holders do not need a visa for Nepal, but as we understand it they do need the restricted area permit for Manaslu and Tsum, at the same fee as other foreigners. They pay the lower SAARC rate of NPR 1,000 for the Manaslu and Annapurna conservation area permits. The licensed guide rule applies equally. Carry your passport rather than a voter ID card, as the permit system works most smoothly with passport details. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
paras: The most frequent problems we see are small: a visa that expires before the trek ends, a name spelled differently on the passport and the application, or plans to change the route mid-trek. Restricted area permits are issued for specific dates and areas, so adding the Tsum Valley or extending in Samagaun after you have set off can cause trouble at checkpoints.

Plan your full itinerary, including spare days for weather, before applying. If you think you may want Manaslu Base Camp, Tsum or a rest day in Bimthang, tell your agency so the permit dates cover it. Keep photocopies of your passport, visa and permits separate from the originals, and photograph them on your phone.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for the Manaslu Circuit?
faqs.a: Yes. You need the Manaslu restricted area permit, the Manaslu Conservation Area Permit, the Annapurna Conservation Area Permit for the Dharapani side and the Tsum Nubri municipality fee. The restricted area permit can only be obtained through a registered agency, and you must trek with a licensed guide.

faqs.q: How much is the Manaslu restricted area permit?
faqs.a: As we understand the 2026 rates, it costs US$100 for the first seven days from September to November plus US$15 per extra day, and US$75 for the first week plus US$10 per day from December to August. Most circuit itineraries pay for eight to ten days. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I trek Manaslu solo in 2026?
faqs.a: According to a Department of Immigration notice in March 2026, solo trekkers can now get restricted area permits without a second person. You still need a licensed guide arranged by a registered agency, so solo means you and your guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I get the Manaslu permit online myself?
faqs.a: No. Only government-registered trekking agencies can apply for restricted area permits on your behalf. They submit your documents to the Department of Immigration, usually after you arrive in Kathmandu with your visa. You provide passport details, photos, insurance and the itinerary.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a restricted area permit for Manaslu?
faqs.a: Yes, as we understand it. Indian nationals need the Manaslu restricted area permit at the same fee as other foreigners and must trek with a licensed guide. They pay the SAARC rate of NPR 1,000 for each conservation area permit. Bring your passport for the application.

Conservation and restricted area permits are checked at several points, including Jagat, Philim or nearby posts, Namrung and the Samagaun area, and the Annapurna permit is checked near Dharapani. Your guide carries the permits and handles checks; keep your passport accessible.

faqs.q: Do I need a TIMS card for Manaslu?
faqs.a: TIMS is officially part of Nepal's trekking system, but for the Manaslu restricted area the key documents are the restricted area permit and conservation permits. Several operators report that TIMS is not issued or checked on Manaslu in practice. Your agency will advise what is currently required.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get the Manaslu permit?
faqs.a: Usually one working day once you are in Kathmandu with a valid visa. Agencies typically apply on the day before you drive to Machha Khola. Immigration offices close on Saturdays and public holidays, so arriving on a Friday evening can delay the start.

faqs.q: Do helicopter passengers need the Manaslu permit?
faqs.a: Yes, if the helicopter lands in Samagaun or elsewhere inside the restricted area. Each foreign passenger needs the restricted area permit and the conservation area permit. Flights that only pass overhead without landing generally do not, as we understand it. Check current status before you travel.
